entry.summary: 1 minute read KONDOR BLUE x Markiplier GoPro MISSION 1 cage system 1:52 KONDOR BLUE has developed a cage and modular rigging system for GoPro’s MISSION 1 cameras with filmmaker and creator Markiplier. KONDOR BLUE has announced a cage and modular rigging system for GoPro’s MISSION
entry.content:
1 minute read
KONDOR BLUE x Markiplier GoPro MISSION 1 cage system
1:52

KONDOR BLUE has developed a cage and modular rigging system for GoPro’s MISSION 1 cameras with filmmaker and creator Markiplier.

KONDOR BLUE has announced a cage and modular rigging system for GoPro’s MISSION 1 cameras, developed with filmmaker and creator Mark Fischbach, rather better known as Markiplier. Fischbach is backing the project with his own investment and has been involved in shaping the product and bringing it to market.

For those of you who remember the fuss over Markiplier’s GoPro investment around the time of the Starman Optical merger, the PR announcing the new cage and system includes a very definite line: “His separate investment in GoPro became public after the collaboration with KONDOR BLUE had already begun.”

(As an aside, GoPro’s latest financials from November 16 were dreadful and showed a $48 million operating loss on $96 million of revenue, with $85 million of debt set against $33.5 million of cash. Despite that, the company says that the proposed merger is still on track.)

System details

The system is designed for MISSION 1, MISSION 1 PRO, and MISSION 1 PRO ILS. The cage has integrated NATO rails on the top and left side, multiple anti-twist mounting points, and a swing-away door for swapping batteries and microSD cards without removing the camera. The cage’s side rib has an integrated carry loop.

A Media I/O Hub adds a full HDMI connection and three USB-C ports for timecode, audio, and power. An optional $80 Power Grip 550 adds a full-hand grip and NP-F550 battery power.

Pricing and availability

The KONDOR BLUE × Markiplier system starts at $100 for the cage only and peaks at $390 for the Pro kit. Pre-orders are open now with shipping expected in January.

entry.title: NANLITE vela 150b, 150c, 300b, 300c: specs and price
entry.summary: 2 minute read NANLITE vela 150b, 150c, 300b, 300c: specs and price 3:25 NANLITE's vela series brings four compact Bowens-mount LED spotlights: 150 W and 300 W, each in bi-color or full-color. All four can run from an AC cable alone. Following their pre-production debut at IBC2026
entry.content:
2 minute read
NANLITE vela 150b, 150c, 300b, 300c: specs and price
3:25

NANLITE's vela series brings four compact Bowens-mount LED spotlights: 150 W and 300 W, each in bi-color or full-color. All four can run from an AC cable alone.

Following their pre-production debut at IBC2026, NANLITE has announced the vela series, four compact LED spotlights: the vela 150b, 150c, 300b, and 300c. All four have a built-in power supply, can run from an AC cable alone, and use a standard Bowens mount. Control is on-board or wireless via the NANLINK App, for individual fixtures or groups.

Size and weight 

The 150b and 150c are 150 W and, NANLITE says, approximately 60% smaller and 60% lighter than traditional spotlights, with a flat 7 cm (2.76 in) profile and a weight of 900 g (1.98 lb). The 300b and 300c are 300 W, approximately 40% smaller and 30% lighter than traditional spotlights, according to NANLITE, with a flat 12 cm (4.72 in) profile and a weight of 2.23 kg (4.92 lb). The 150b and 150c have a detachable mounting bracket with 180° tilt, a 5/8" baby pin receiver, and a 1/4"-20 mounting point for the optional battery grip or a compatible bracket.

Output and CCT range

Output at 1 m (3.3 ft) and 5600 K is 52,600 lux for the 150b and 44,200 lux for the 150c (Fresnel lens at 21°), and up to 66,600 lux for the 300b and 52,200 lux for the 300c (40° reflector).

The 150b and 300b cover 2700 K to 7500 K, while the 150c and 300c use the Nebula C4 Light Engine and cover 2400 K to 12,000 K with ±150 green/magenta adjustment. CRI/TLCI averages are 96/98 and 95/94 for the b and c models, respectively.

Optics, softboxes, and power options

The 150b and 150c include a Fresnel lens (21° to 40° adjustable beam) and a diffuser. The 300b and 300c include a 40° reflector. Two octagonal softboxes are available: the SB-O-40 for all four lights and the SB-O-30 for the 150b and 150c only.

All four support AC power. The 150b and 150c also support a PD 3.1 adapter or power bank, a battery grip, and a 14.4 V to 14.8 V V-mount battery via the D-Tap to USB-C PD adapter cable. The optional BT-BG-14.4V73 battery grip, available for the 150b and 150c, provides approximately 45 minutes of runtime at 65% maximum brightness.

The 150b and 300b come in Mint Blue, and the 150c and 300c in Serene Blue. Each comes with a carrying bag with built-in compartments.

Pricing and availability

Prices are $209 USD for the vela 150b (2-light kit $369), $249 for the 150c (2-light kit $459), $299 for the 300b, and $349 for the 300c. The lights are shipping now, with 20% off available for Black Friday.

entry.content:
3 minute read
OBSBOT Tail Air 2 and Tail 2 ADV: specs and price
6:09

Tail Air 2 gets a 1-inch sensor and 4K60. Tail 2 ADV adds 21x optical zoom. Both record OBSBOT Log and go on sale December 8.

OBSBOT has added two cameras to its PTZR lineup: the Tail Air 2, which gains a roll axis and a 1-inch sensor, and the Tail 2 ADV, which adds 21x optical zoom.

Tail Air 2: 1-inch sensor, Log, and 3D LUTs

The Tail Air 2 is an AI-powered PTZR camera with a 1-inch CMOS sensor (3.2 μm pixels), an f/1.9 aperture, and an eight-element optical lens. It records 4K60 and 1080p120. A dedicated AI imaging chip handles low-light noise reduction, while LOFIC HDR supports up to 13 stops of dynamic range under HDR recording conditions at up to 30 fps. Sensitivity reaches ISO 25,600 with HDR disabled. All-Pixel Phase Detection Autofocus (PDAF) offers Global Focus, Foreground Focus, and Face Focus modes.

Both cameras introduce OBSBOT Log, the company's proprietary 8-bit Log recording profile and the first in an OBSBOT camera. Custom 3D LUTs can be previewed through OBSBOT Center, OBSBOT Start, and OBSBOT Live while filming or streaming.

AI tracking, roll axis, and vertical 4K

AI Tracking 2.0 recognizes people, more than 30 animal species, and over 200 object categories. Users double-click a subject or draw a selection box to choose what to track, and the software offers several tracking modes. Single-Person Tracking reacquires a briefly obscured subject; Group Tracking adjusts camera angle and framing as people move or enter and leave the shot; Face Framing leaves space in the direction a subject faces; and Auto Zoom maintains a selected full-body, medium, or close-up framing as distance changes.

Tracking speed, single-axis movement, active tracking zones, and subject positioning are adjustable. Upgraded AI Director Grids switch between AI Tracking, Preset, and Launchpad in one interface. Gesture Control lets users control tracking, zoom, and recording from up to 5 m (16 ft) away.

A dedicated Roll axis adds rotation to Pan, Tilt, and Zoom. Launchpad 2.0 provides eight preset camera movements and two customizable modes, and an Auto Leveling System corrects camera orientation to keep the horizon level on uneven surfaces. For vertical content, the lens module physically rotates 90 degrees to capture native vertical 4K60 without cropping the sensor's full imaging area.

Connectivity, battery, and sync

The camera is built around a native IP architecture and supports SRT, RTSP, and RTMP, plus NDI HX3 through the NDI-enabled version or a separately purchased license, over WiFi 6 or wired Ethernet. Control options are VISCA, OSC, Stream Deck, and an Open SDK. Physical connections are a 3.5 mm audio input, a Micro HDMI output, and two USB-C ports for power and data. It records locally to microSD cards up to 1 TB and has a built-in microphone and Bluetooth connectivity with the OBSBOT Vox SE wireless microphone.

A built-in 2630 mAh battery lasts up to 205 minutes at 1080p30, with USB PD 3.0 fast charging. Timecode (with compatible external timecode equipment) and Precision Time Protocol (PTP) synchronization are supported for multi-camera work.

Tail 2 ADV: 21x optical zoom and variable aperture

The Tail 2 ADV has a 21x optical zoom, the longest in the OBSBOT lineup, plus a 40x hybrid zoom, via a 12-element optical lens system and a custom lens motor. The body measures approximately 10 cm (4 in) wide and 15 cm (6 in) tall. A custom 1/2-inch CMOS sensor with Dual Native ISO records 4K60 and 1080p120, with AI-ISP noise reduction in low light. HDR is supported at 4K30 with All-Pixel PDAF enabled, but not at 4K60. Focus Over Zooming helps the camera refocus on distant, stationary subjects as focal length changes.

A physical variable aperture runs from f/1.7 to f/7.0 at the wide end and from f/3.8 to f/7.0 at the telephoto end. In Pro Mode, aperture is set manually, and ISO and shutter speed can each be set to Auto or Manual.

AI Tracking 2.0 works at distances of up to 240 m (787 ft), compared with 95 m (312 ft) on the Tail 2, and adds six tracking-speed settings (including a Custom mode with independent Pan and Tilt speeds), Axis Control, Composition Lines, and Zone Tracking. Otherwise the ADV shares the Tail Air 2's tracking modes, OBSBOT Log and LUT previews, Timecode and PTP sync, native vertical 4K60, and IP and control protocols, adding an official OBSBOT Log-to-Rec.709 LUT and Pelco-D/P control.

The ADV's connections include 3G-SDI output up to 1080p60, full-size HDMI 2.0 output up to 4K, Gigabit Ethernet, a 2.5 mm RS-232 port, separate 3.5 mm microphone and line inputs, dual-band WiFi 6, and PoE+ for power and network over one cable. FreeD output supplies camera movement and lens data for AR, XR, and virtual studio workflows, and a dual-color Tally indicator shows red Program and green Preview status in compatible NDI workflows. Gimbal angular jitter is as low as ±0.0005°, the Auto Leveling System also works in inverted or non-standard mounting positions, and a built-in 5000 mAh battery lasts up to 4 hours 36 minutes.

Pricing and release dates 

The Tail Air 2 lists at $899 for the Non-NDI version and $999 for the NDI version, with a $100 pre-order discount taking them to $799 and $899. The Tail 2 ADV lists at $1599, or $1399 with the pre-order discount. All go on sale December 8 through the OBSBOT online store, Amazon US, and select retailers worldwide.

entry.title: Fujifilm X-T6: X Summit Paris set for December 2, here's what we know so far
entry.summary: 3 minute read Fujifilm X-T6: X Summit Paris set for December 2, here's what we know so far 3:15 Fujifilm has confirmed an X Summit in Paris on December 2, and the X-T6 is widely expected to be launched there. Rumors point to a 40 MP sensor, new AI autofocus, and possible 8K video
entry.content:
3 minute read
Fujifilm X-T6: X Summit Paris set for December 2, here's what we know so far
3:15

Fujifilm has confirmed an X Summit in Paris on December 2, and the X-T6 is widely expected to be launched there. Rumors point to a 40 MP sensor, new AI autofocus, and possible 8K video.

Update, November 19: Fujifilm has confirmed that its next X Summit will take place in Paris on Wednesday, December 2, streamed live on YouTube from 10:00 CET (09:00 GMT, 04:00 EST). Fujifilm has not said what it will announce, but the date in Fujifilm’s teaser video ends with the “6” turning red, which is about a big a clue as you;re going to get. Expect the X-T6 to be announced, though when it will actually ship is up in the air still. The accompanying XF 50-140mm f/2.8 II lens should appear too.

Here's how we got to where we are. Like many camera stories this year, it's not been entirely straightforward.

Update, October 31: Fujirumors said the X-T6 was scheduled for November, with a component shortage blamed for the September delay. The XF 50-140mm f/2.8 II is expected to launch alongside it. Fujifilm confirmed none of this at the time. Leaked sketches show recessed top-plate dials, a single four-way D-pad, and a three-way tilt screen, with no vertical battery grip connector. The new NP-W255 battery is reportedly rated at 2550 mAh, around 16% more than the current NP-W235. Photo Rumors expects European pricing of €1999 to €2199.

Given the nigh-mythical status of its 2022 predecessor, the Fujifilm X-T6 is easily one of the most anticipated cameras of what is shaping up, by rumor anyway, to be a very fecund season for new camera releases. The only issue is that, until now, the one thing we knew with any certainty was that it was delayed. Fujifilm has now confirmed a launch event, although it hasn't said what it will show.

Fujifilm had an X Summit planned for early September, ostensibly to launch the X-T6, and there were some other events such as a B&H Photo "Fujifilm Experience" demo event on September 8 in New York that gave credence to that theory. But that X Summit was taken off the schedules with no new date, and everything else faded into the background as well. The December 2 date, confirmed on November 18, is the first firm sign of movement.

Fujirumors had pointed to November and blamed a component shortage for the delay, though Fujifilm has never commented on the reason. Earlier speculation ranged from time required to lock down new software features, with a new AI autofocus system and film simulations name-checked, to component issues.

So, what can we expect to see when it finally is announced?

Likely features

Though still primarily stills-focused, the new AF as well as a rumored boost to 8K makes it of more interest to video shooters than perhaps before. Plus being from the same stable as the currently very well-regarded GFX range is not going to harm its appeal in the slightest.

The sensor looks like it is staying at 40 MP, though whether that will be the existing sensor from the X-T5 coupled with a new imaging processor or a wholly new model is currently a matter of some speculation. A new X Processor 6 is more definite, and helps supply those previously mentioned AF improvements. It will also play a role in adding new film simulations, bringing the total count up to 21.

8K120 video has been mooted, but the excellent Fujirumors, which as you would expect is all over this, reckons that framerate is implausible.

A new battery, the NP-W255, is reportedly rated at 2550 mAh, around 16% more than the NP-W235, which should mean longer shooting times. It is said to be compatible with older X-series bodies. The screen and viewfinder look to be unchanged from the X-T5.

Pricing and availability

Price? The X-T5 launched at $1699 and its successor is expected to be anything on a scale from the same (unlikely given everything that's going on in the industry at the moment) to a slightly more likely $1999. This is especially true as tariffs have driven the US pricing of the camera up to that level already. Photo Rumors puts European pricing at €1999 to €2199.

Availability? Under normal circumstances, Fujifilm starts shipping the X-T series only a couple of weeks after it is announced, so if the X-T6 appears on December 2, expect shipping in mid to late December at the earliest. German outlet Photografix reports that sources expect pre-orders to open on announcement day, but that is unconfirmed.

entry.title: Density 1.0 color grading plugin for Final Cut Pro
entry.summary: 3 minute read Density 1.0 color grading plugin for Final Cut Pro 5:16 Density 1.0 is a color grading and film emulation plugin for Final Cut Pro on Apple silicon Macs. Launch price is $169, with a free seven-day trial. Density 1.0 is an interesting new color grading plugin for Fi
entry.content:
3 minute read
Density 1.0 color grading plugin for Final Cut Pro
5:16

Density 1.0 is a color grading and film emulation plugin for Final Cut Pro on Apple silicon Macs. Launch price is $169, with a free seven-day trial.

Density 1.0 is an interesting new color grading plugin for Final Cut Pro on Apple silicon Macs, developed by filmmaker and YouTuber Pascal Basel, which looks to bring a complete color grading workflow to the app.

Basel has edited in Final Cut Pro for more than 12 years. “What I wanted was a properly color-managed pipeline inside Final Cut Pro, with film emulation that works in both HDR and SDR,” he says.

Here is how the workflow runs.

Auto Setup, effect stacks, and camera input

Set up the timeline. Clip Board lays out every clip in the edit as a card, which lets editors locate and pick shots without searching the timeline by hand. Effects, groups, and looks can go onto a chosen set of clips, onto everything in the current view (once a search or filter has been applied, say), or onto the full timeline. Auto Setup handles all of it in a single step. It adds the effects, detects each clip’s Log profile and applies the matching input transform, sets the Output from the project, creates the groups, and, if selected, applies ML Auto Balance, an editable starting point for exposure and white balance.

Assemble your own effect stack. Editors choose which effects each clip receives. Within Add Effect Stack and Auto Setup, they select from Density’s four main effects (Input, Clip Grade, Look Grade, and Output) and can place Density Tools or Final Cut Pro’s native color effects, Color Wheels for example, between them. Set as Default saves the stack for the next run, and it can be applied to a chosen set of clips, to everything in the current view, or to the full timeline.

Convert each camera. Input sits first in every clip’s effect chain. It transforms the camera’s flat Log footage into the working color space, applying the input transform that corresponds to the camera’s Log profile. For many cameras, Density reads the Log profile from the file, so every clip is assigned the correct transform automatically. The plugin ships with 27 camera Log profiles. For the remainder, an Input Rule, such as “file names containing SL3 are Sony S-Log3,” does the job. Grade Health marks clips that have an incorrect Log profile or a missing effect, and provides a fix.

Grading groups, color style, and film emulation

Grade scenes as a unit. Groups allow related shots to share a single grade with no adjustment layers. In Clip Grade, a group shares corrections wrapped around each clip’s own layer, which means an outlier shot can still be corrected individually. In Look Grade, the group shares the entire look. Primaries, wheels, curves, and Hue / Sat / Luma (which adjusts one color at a time) live in Final Cut Pro’s Inspector, where masks and keyframes behave as they normally do.

Craft the look. Color Style points a shot’s colors in a particular direction. Tint assigns palette colors to different tonal ranges, for instance teal in the shadows and orange in the highlights. Pull shifts the colors already present in the shot toward the palette. Shades and Greens fine-tune individual colors and foliage, and Protect Neutrals and Protect Skin keep grays clean and skin looking natural.

Film Lab constructs film emulation as a negative printed onto a print stock, selected from 57 film stocks, with push / pull processing and printer lights that set the print’s color balance. The 72 bundled presets fill these controls, and a completed look can be exported as a LUT.

Finishing tools and SDR and HDR output

Add finishing tools. Seventeen Density Tools, each handling one task, work as individual effects on any clip:

  • Time-lapse flicker and color drift: Deflicker & Color Stabilizer
  • Matching: Chromatic Adaptation, Palette Compressor
  • Shaping: Dehaze / Atmosphere, Glow / Pop, Midtone Detail, Diffusion / Mist
  • Film texture: Halation, Bloom, Film Grain, Gate Weave, Vignette
  • Grading and LUTs: Wheels, Curves, HSLD Tools, HSL Curves, LUT Look

Deliver in SDR and HDR. Output readies the finished grade for its target display: Rec.709 SDR, P3-D65, Rec.2020 PQ, or Rec.2020 HLG. All cameras are graded in a single wide working space, either DaVinci Wide Gamut or ACES, so a new delivery format calls only for a new Output setting.

Pricing and availability

Density is a perpetual license sold at density.film for $269, with a launch price of $169 until November 29. Anyone who activates a free trial by then keeps it through their seven-day trial. The trial includes every feature, with no watermark and no credit card required. Each license covers personal and paid client work on two Macs and includes 24 months of updates. After that, an optional $39 Update Pass adds 12 more months. Refunds are available within 14 days.

Density requires an Apple silicon Mac (M1 or later), macOS 26.6 or later, and Final Cut Pro 12.4 or later. It is not available for Intel Macs or Final Cut Pro for iPad.

entry.title: LUMIX SHX1 cage: Wooden Camera range
entry.summary: 2 minute read LUMIX SHX1 cage: Wooden Camera range 3:15 Wooden Camera's cage and accessory range for the LUMIX SHX1 is built to switch between horizontal and vertical. Wooden Camera is first out of the blocks with a cage and accessory collection for the new LUMIX SHX1 . Component
entry.content:
2 minute read
LUMIX SHX1 cage: Wooden Camera range
3:15

Wooden Camera's cage and accessory range for the LUMIX SHX1 is built to switch between horizontal and vertical.

Wooden Camera is first out of the blocks with a cage and accessory collection for the new LUMIX SHX1. Components are sold individually or as complete systems, and have been designed around the camera's ability to shoot both horizontally and vertically.

“The Panasonic AU-SHX1 is built to shoot both horizontally and vertically, so we built an accessory ecosystem that makes switching between the two as fast as possible,” says Dominick Aiello, Divisional Senior Director of Accessories at Wooden Camera. “Keeping the lens centered and taking weight out wherever we could were a given. What sets this collection apart is how quickly you can reconfigure, with NATO rails and ARCA mounting wherever they make sense. We also sweated the small details, like integrated QD points and film-plane markings, that make life on set a little easier.”

The ARCA Riser Plate sets the lens-centered height for accessories and integrates an adjustable lens support for lens mount adapters. Mounting points along its sides and bottom support both orientations.

Switching orientations

In vertical mode, the side plates take over as the camera's base and top. The Right Side Plate becomes the base. Paired with the Universal ARCA Dovetail, the Right Side Plate lets the camera rotate onto its side and lock back onto the baseplate. The Left Side Plate becomes the top. Its asymmetric shape sets its rail at lens-center height, and it accepts the native handle, lens motors, and supports. It carries film-plane markings.

The Top Plate adds 360° Quick Disconnect points for camera straps, plus mounting points for the Top Plate Dual Rod Clamp. It is compatible with the native handle or the Ultra Handle system.

Power and handle accessories

The D-Box power hub supports a V-Mount or Gold Mount battery, with P-Tap outputs for accessories, DC-IN for continuous power, and an electronic fuse for overload protection. A D-Box Support Bracket secures it to the Riser Plate.

An XLR NATO Bracket moves the XLR unit onto NATO clamps. The Native Handle to NATO Clamp Adapter adds a lever-lock release, so the handle can be installed, removed, or repositioned without tools. The Dual Rod Native Handle Adapter adds dual 15 mm (0.6 in) LWS rods for lens motors and other accessories.

Systems, pre-orders, and pricing

Components are sold individually or as complete systems that will ship in the following configurations:

  • Base Plate System: ARCA Riser Plate and ARCA Baseplate.
  • Core Cage System: adds the Top Plate, Right Side Plate, and Universal ARCA Dovetail.
  • Elite Cage System: adds the Left Side Plate, a NATO rail, the Ultra Handle system, and Quick Disconnect points.
  • Native Handle Upgrade Kit: adds NATO mounting, rod support, and XLR unit repositioning.

Pre-orders for the collection begin in December. Pricing is to be announced, but you can sign up for updates on Wooden Camera's SHX1 page. If you want an indication of costs, the company's Sony FX5 cage system released last month went from $99 to $799.

entry.title: Panasonic LUMIX SHX1: specs, price, and release date
entry.summary: 4 minute read Panasonic LUMIX SHX1: specs, price, and release date 6:49 Panasonic has announced the LUMIX SHX1, a 6K full-frame box cinema camera that neatly encapsulates the merger of the company’s professional AV and consumer imaging businesses. It arrives in December for $4699
entry.content:
4 minute read
Panasonic LUMIX SHX1: specs, price, and release date
6:49

Panasonic has announced the LUMIX SHX1, a 6K full-frame box cinema camera that neatly encapsulates the merger of the company’s professional AV and consumer imaging businesses. It arrives in December for $4699.

We have been wondering for a while how Panasonic will celebrate the 25th anniversary of its LUMIX brand, and now we know. The company has officially announced the LUMIX SHX1 (AU-SHX1), the first compact cinema camera in LUMIX history.

In such a leak-dominated industry, this has come right out of left field with only a brief teaser released Monday, November 16, hinting at what was to come.

6K full-frame sensor, 15 stops, and ARRI LogC3

The LUMIX SHX1 is a full-frame box-style camera with a 6K (about 24.1 MP) partially stacked CMOS sensor and an optical low-pass filter. Dual Native ISO and Dynamic Range Boost give 15 stops of dynamic range in V-Log, with caveats: 14+ stops with Boost off, and with it on, video quality and ISO sensitivity are limited and rolling-shutter distortion increases. ARRI LogC3 is pre-installed alongside V-Log, with the ARRI Look Library (log-to-log).

It's nothing if not versatile. Panasonic pitches it as everything from an A camera with cinematic image quality and the compact versatility of a mirrorless system to a highly modular B camera or even a PTZ camera that can give users full-frame quality with easy multi-camera control.

Blackmagic RAW and ProRes RAW recording

The camera records Blackmagic RAW directly to an external USB SSD, a first for LUMIX. Blackmagic color science can also be selected, and footage edits in DaVinci Resolve without conversion. Apple ProRes RAW HQ / ProRes RAW records internally to a CFexpress Type B card with no external recorder, a setup Panasonic says suits gimbal, solo, and documentary shooting.

Open Gate Blackmagic RAW 6K24, with a slight crop, is another first for the LUMIX line. 6K30 / 5.1K60 4:2:0 10-bit and 3.8K48 4:2:2 10-bit (new) are also supported.

The SSD can be up to 2 TB and must be USB Type-C compatible. It's worth noting that recording to it rules out simultaneous recording to SD or CFexpress, though a proxy file can go to an SD card.

The anamorphic desqueeze display now supports vertical shooting for “Vertiscope” framing, with Phase Hybrid AF remaining active.

Autofocus and stabilization

Phase Hybrid AF has 779 focus points, and AI detection covers eyes and faces, including tilted or partly hidden faces. Tracking AF follows the selected person when others cross in front of the camera, though it may select another subject with similar clothes, colors, or posture, or if the subject is hidden for a prolonged period. Real-time recognition AF covers eyes, faces, bodies, Urban Sports, animals, cars, motorcycles, bicycles, airplanes, and trains.

The 5-axis B.I.S. works with lenses that lack O.I.S., and Dual I.S. 2 combines camera and lens stabilization at telephoto focal lengths. Active I.S. and E.I.S. work together while walking, with a cropless E.I.S. mode for wide-angle lenses and a mode for anamorphic shooting that includes roll correction.

Body, monitor, and connections

The aluminum and magnesium alloy body weighs about 984 g (2.17 lb), body only. As you would expect from the adaptable form factor, it can be rigged for horizontal or vertical shooting. The 3.0-inch, about 1.84-million-dot touch monitor is top-mounted, tilts upward or swings out to the side, and is another first for LUMIX.

The camera records 4K120 without time limits within the guaranteed operating temperature range, using a metal body, a large cooling fan, and a dedicated thermal system. Given the limits often associated with compact  bodies, this is impressive.

Dual card slots take CFexpress Type B and SD cards, with a lock lever on the card door. Outputs are 12G-SDI (up to 4K60) and HDMI Type A. A BNC TC IN/OUT terminal syncs timecode, and Bluetooth timecode sync is also supported. Internal 32-bit float audio recording through the 3.5 mm microphone input and Micro V-mount battery support are both firsts for LUMIX.

Two locking USB Type-C ports handle USB-SSD connection and USB Power Delivery, which requires a 100 W or higher (5 A/20 V) USB AC adaptor and cable. Two further terminals serve optional accessories.

Controls include the LUMIX triple-button layout for WB, ISO, and IRIS, an AF ON button, and front and rear tally lamps. Exposure tools are Waveform Monitor, Vectorscope, Spot Luminance Meter, Zebra Pattern, Histogram, and False Color. View Assist applies LUTs (preset Vlog_709 / ARRI709 or custom) to the displayed image, including via HDMI. Live streaming runs over WiFi or USB tethering with a smartphone.

Accessories, firmware, and apps

Two optional accessories are available at launch. The XLR Handle Unit AU-XHU1 enables 4ch 32-bit float audio with the camera's 3.5 mm stereo mini jack, plus 96 kHz/24-bit recording. The XLR unit and top handle can be used separately, and the AU-XHU1 has a cold shoe and screw holes.

The Control Grip AU-GRP1 has WB/ISO/IRIS buttons, a joystick, an Fn button, a power-zoom-compatible zoom rocker (Crop Zoom for lenses without Power Zoom), an ARRI-standard rosette mount with rotation, and wired remote control.

The Live Production Unit AU-LPU1, due in the first half of 2027, has a common IP control protocol for Panasonic PTZ systems, a Genlock IN terminal, and a PoE++ LAN terminal.

A firmware update in the same period adds control of the Tilta Mirage Variable ND from the AU-GRP1 and Panasonic controllers, plus Tilta hand wheel control of focus and iris on L-Mount lenses. The ND control requires a USB Type-C connection to the Tilta Nucleus 2.4G Wireless Control Hub (Panasonic).

Panasonic says it is also developing a power zoom lens for the camera.

LUMIX Flow Ver. 1.8.0 and LUMIX Lab Ver. 3.2.0 add SHX1 support and support for iOS 27 and Android 17. Flow also adds Frame Preview, Smartphone Sync Recording, and Sequential Play (SHX1 only), plus a new client remote-review feature.

Pricing and availability

The LUMIX SHX1 will be available from December 2026 at $4699 / €5199 / £4399. The AU-XHU1 (€649 / £549) and AU-GRP1 (€499 / £419) are also due in December 2026, while a kit that includes both will be available for $5499. The camera comes with the LUMIX 5-Year Warranty, and will appear in the Try Before Buy Program (a free 48-hour loan) soon.

entry.content:
1 minute read
RED Connect and Colorfront color management
1:50

Colorfront's color engine is now native to RED Connect, meaning that live 8K R3D feeds can be graded and mapped to SDR and HDR in real time.

RED Digital Cinema and Colorfront have partnered to integrate native Colorfront color management into the RED Connect camera module, allowing users to apply the Colorfront Engine to 8K live RED camera feeds. That means productions already using Colorfront for color management, SDR/HDR workflows, or finishing and delivery can now bring RED Connect sources directly into those workflows. There are a fair few of them too, especially as the engine is a powerful option for AJA kit, including the newly released FS8.

The integration provides color grading and SDR/HDR mapping of RAW R3D files in real time, with playout in HD, 4K, and 8K. Colorfront's Perceptual Processing technology uses models of the human vision system to create a default image. A single-master workflow avoids complex LUTs and allows SDR and HDR outputs to be generated from the same source while preserving artistic intent across all deliverables.

The system is built around a broadcast-optimized version of the Colorfront Engine. It offers Lift, Gamma, and Gain parameters, alongside HDR and look management tools. Operators can shade digital cinema cameras through a familiar interface while taking advantage of the dynamic range, wide color gamut, and global shutter performance of RED Digital Cinema cameras.

The partnership will also allow productions to move RAW R3D content across IP networks while maintaining the same color science throughout the workflow, which is always a good option to take

Colorfront Color Management is available now for RED Connect, with pricing TBA. More information: https://engine.colorfront.cloud/

entry.summary: 2 minute read Sony drone boom mic patent: stays out of shot 2:51 Sony's patent application describes a drone that positions a mic as close to an actor as possible without entering the shot. What could go wrong? One day when we have spare time, we're going to create a website call
entry.content:
2 minute read
Sony drone boom mic patent: stays out of shot
2:51

Sony's patent application describes a drone that positions a mic as close to an actor as possible without entering the shot. What could go wrong?

One day when we have spare time, we're going to create a website called Boom! that captures boom mics straying into shots where they are not wanted, like unintended UFOs descending from the studio lights. It will never not be funny. In the meantime, though, we will just have to appreciate the art of the boom operator who, most of the time anyway, manages to keep the mic out of shot while capturing pristine audio.

US 2026/0352998 A1, published on November 5, 2026, and brought to our attention by Patentlyze, ups the ante by mounting a boom mic on a drone. The company behind the application, Sony, seems to have put a lot of thought into how it will operate.

The system uses two zones. The first covers whatever the lens can see; the second is the recordable range, where the microphone can still pick up direct speech. The drone is told to sit inside the second zone and outside the first, as near to the actor as it can get, with the mic's sound axis pointed at them. As the actor moves, it recalculates its position.

Avoiding lights, people, and its own noise

The filing goes beyond basic hovering skills and describes a system that will avoid noise sources such as air conditioners and generators, keep clear of studio lights so it does not throw a shadow into shot, and, of course, steer around people. A crew member can set a position by hand, and the system stores it so the same placement can be recreated for rehearsals and retakes.

The drone is something of a noise source in itself, but the filing proposes that this is a known quantity. The system stores the propeller rotation speed and can filter that hum out of the recording. How the actors will cope with the incessant buzz, though, is perhaps a more pertinent question.

The drone can aim at the midpoint between two speakers, pivot a directional mic between them based on script timing, use an omnidirectional mic, or carry two directional mics. The application even suggests a second drone can hold up the mic cable to keep it out of frame.

Coming to a set near you?

Of course, the chances of it actually entering production are slim. Tech companies file patents constantly. Others from Sony published the same day included one for blowing scents around an automobile interior in response to driving past a billboard, and fan attachments for an HMD so gamers could sense wind direction when in virtual worlds. And that's just the air-related stuff.

But somewhere out there now, there's at least one boom operator looking at their kit, firing up the DJI website, calculating payloads, and wondering if it could work.

entry.content:
1 minute read
Lomography Lomo72: price, specs, release date
1:49

The Lomo72 is a half-frame 35mm film camera with a multi-coated glass lens. It shoots up to 72 photos per roll, costs $79, and ships in December.

With half-frame cameras among the surprise hits of recent years, notably theFujifilm X half, Lomography has announced its own version, the Lomo72. 

The Lomo72 splits a standard 35mm frame in two, giving up to 72 photos per roll, hence the name. It takes any standard 35mm film and provides an exposure area of 17 × 24 mm.

It is all fairly bare bones, as you would expect from Lomography, though is a step up from the Simple Use half-frame camera it launched in July. The lens is a 27mm affair, featuring 2 elements in 2 groups fixed at f/10. Shutter speeds are either Bulb (B) or 1/100 (N), though for all its blunt approach the camera supports unlimited multiple exposures and long exposures. Focus is resolutely manual and set to either Close (0.4 to 1 m, 1.3 to 3.3 ft) or Infinity.

Flash carry

The camera comes in black or silver and has a multi-coated glass lens sitting on the front of a pleasingly retro-style metal-plated body A built-in flash with colored filters has a range of 1 m (3.3 ft) at ISO 100 and 2 m (6.6 ft) at ISO 400. It runs on a single AAA (1.5 V) battery. The camera has a standard ¼" tripod mount and a cable release thread. Lomography is also keen to highlight that it comes with a neck strap. In other words, the pitch is that this is a camera to be seen with as much as used.

Pricing and availability

The Lomo72 costs $79. Pre-orders are open now with both versions expected to ship in December 2026.
